lessons.title: Video streaming (YouTube / Netflix)
lessons.summary: Design a video platform end to end, covering resumable upload, a chunked transcoding pipeline, adaptive bitrate with HLS/DASH, and a CDN strategy like Netflix Open Connect.
lessons.body:
Video streaming is the classic "bandwidth is the system" design. The metadata service is a fairly ordinary CRUD app. What makes it hard is the **bytes**: petabytes arriving every day that must be transcoded, and hundreds of petabytes leaving every day that must reach phones on flaky 4G without stalling.

A strong answer spends little time on the metadata tables and most of its time on three pipelines: **upload → transcode → deliver**.

## Requirements

### Functional
- Creators upload videos (up to several hours long, many GB).
- Viewers watch on any device, with playback that adapts to their network.
- Search and browse metadata: title, description, thumbnails.
- Record view counts and watch progress ("resume where you left off").

### Non-functional
- **Playback start under 2 s**, and rebuffering kept to a tiny fraction of watch time. This is the metric that drives engagement.
- **Very high availability for playback.** A short delay in a new upload becoming watchable is fine; failed playback is not.
- **Durability**: never lose an uploaded original.
- Read-heavy: views outnumber uploads by many orders of magnitude.
- Cost matters a lot. Egress and transcoding compute are the main bills.

Clarify scope early. YouTube-style means a huge long tail of user uploads. Netflix-style means a small, curated catalogue (tens of thousands of titles) watched by a huge audience. The CDN strategy is very different for each.

## Back-of-the-envelope

Assume a YouTube-scale platform.

**Uploads.** In 2019 YouTube said that more than 500 hours of video were uploaded every minute. Use that dated figure as an illustrative planning input, not a measurement of current upload volume.

```
500 h/min x 1,440 min = 720,000 h/day
Source at ~10 Mbps (1080p):
  10e6 b/s x 3,600 s / 8 = 4.5 GB/hour
720,000 x 4.5 GB = ~3.2 PB/day originals
```

For a hypothetical storage model, assume additional renditions bring total new storage to **6–8 PB/day**. This multiplier depends on the actual ladders/codecs and is not a measured YouTube ratio. Over a year that is 365 x 6–8 PB, or **about 2–3 EB**, before replication. These are deliberately rough: real sources range from 5 Mbps phone clips to 50+ Mbps 4K. Clip duration does not itself reduce the assumed bytes per hour; source bitrate and format determine that.

**Viewing.** Say 200 M daily viewers each watching 1 hour at an average 3 Mbps.

```
Average concurrent viewers:
  200 M x 1 h / 24 h = ~8.3 M
Peak (about 2x average) = ~17 M
Peak egress: 17 M x 3 Mbps = ~50 Tbps
Daily egress:
  200 M x 3,600 s x 3 Mbps / 8 = ~270 PB
```

Serving 50 Tbps to a global audience makes geographic distribution, network capacity and egress cost central design concerns. A CDN also reduces network distance; 50 Tbps is not a universal single-data-centre limit.

**Transcoding.** As a working assumption (it varies hugely with presets and hardware), assume15 core-hours per source hour across the chosen ladder. This is a hypothetical input, not a hardware/codec benchmark.

```
720,000 h/day x 15 core-h
  = 10.8 M core-h/day
/ 24 = ~450,000 cores running non-stop
```

Even if the assumption is off by 2x either way, the answer is hundreds of thousands of cores. This is why platforms spend expensive codecs (AV1, heavy VP9 presets) on videos that actually get watched.

## API design

```
POST /v1/uploads
  { title, size_bytes, content_type }
  -> { upload_id, upload_url }

PUT  {upload_url}
  Content-Range: bytes 0-8388607/...
  (GCS-style resumable chunks, e.g. 8 MiB)

POST /v1/uploads/{id}/complete
  -> { video_id, status: "processing" }

GET  /v1/videos/{video_id}
  -> metadata, status, thumbnails

GET  /v1/videos/{video_id}/play
  -> { manifest_url (signed, CDN),
       drm_licence_url }

POST /v1/videos/{video_id}/progress
  { position_s }
```

Two points matter here. First, the upload URL points straight at **object storage** (a pre-signed S3/GCS URL or a resumable-upload endpoint), so multi-GB bodies never pass through your API servers. Second, `/play` doesn't stream video. It returns a **manifest URL** on the CDN, and the player does the rest.

## Data model

| Store | What lives there |
|---|---|
| Sharded SQL | videos, channels, renditions |
| Object store | originals, segments |
| Wide-column / KV | watch progress, counters |
| Search index | titles, tags, captions |

```
videos(video_id PK, owner_id, title,
       status, duration_s, created_at)
renditions(video_id, codec, height,
           bitrate_kbps, manifest_path)
watch_progress(user_id, video_id,
               position_s, updated_at)
```

YouTube scaled its MySQL metadata tier by building Vitess, a sharding layer that is now an open-source CNCF project. Shard `videos` by `video_id` and `watch_progress` by `user_id`, because the access patterns are "load this video" and "load this user's history".

## High-level architecture

```
 Creator                          Viewer
    |                               |
    v                               v
+--------+   +-------+        +---------+
| Upload |-->| Blob  |        |   CDN   |
|  API   |   | store |        |  edge   |
+--------+   +-------+        +---------+
    |            |  ^               | miss
    v            v  |               v
+--------+   +---------+      +---------+
| Queue  |-->|Transcode|      | Origin/ |
| (jobs) |   | workers |----->| shield  |
+--------+   +---------+      +---------+
    |
    v
+----------+  +--------+
| Metadata |  | Search |
|   DB     |  | index  |
+----------+  +--------+
```

## Deep dive 1: the upload and transcoding pipeline

### Resumable upload

A 4 GB upload from a phone *will* get interrupted. Use a resumable protocol (Google's resumable upload API, tus, or S3 multipart). Offset-based protocols such as tus/GCS resumable upload report committed offsets. S3 multipart instead tracks an upload ID, numbered parts and their returned ETags/checksums; parts can arrive out of order and retry individually. A generic presigned S3 PUT does not implement a Content-Range resumable session.

When the upload completes, the storage service fires an event ("object created") onto a queue. Don't have the client call the transcoder directly. The queue makes the pipeline durable and lets you absorb upload spikes.

### Split, transcode in parallel, stitch

Encoding a 2-hour film serially on one machine takes hours. Instead:

1. **Validate and probe** the file (container, codec, duration, corrupt frames).
2. **Split** it into chunks of a few seconds, cut on keyframe (GOP) boundaries using independently decodable boundaries (such as closed GOPs/appropriate random-access points), aligned across renditions. An arbitrary keyframe in an open GOP may still depend on other frames.
3. **Fan out** one task per (chunk × rendition) to a worker pool. A 2-hour film in 4 s chunks across 6 renditions is about 10,800 tasks, giving parallel work units; completion time depends on actual encoder throughput, available workers, input decoding and assembly.
4. **Assemble** the outputs into packaged segments and write the manifests.
5. Generate thumbnails, run content checks (copyright matching, safety classifiers) and extract captions in parallel branches.
6. Mark the video `ready` in the metadata DB.

Model this as a **DAG** of tasks with a workflow engine. Every task must be **idempotent**, keyed on video/source version, chunk, rendition and encoding profile. Publish only complete validated outputs, using immutable attempt objects plus an atomic winning-result pointer or conditional writes. A deterministic path alone cannot stop a stale attempt overwriting a newer encode.

### The bitrate ladder

An illustrative H.264 ladder (not a universal recommendation):

| Rendition | Bitrate |
|---|---|
| 240p | 0.3 Mbps |
| 480p | 1.0 Mbps |
| 720p | 2.5 Mbps |
| 1080p | 5 Mbps |
| 2160p (4K) | 15 Mbps |

Netflix moved from one fixed ladder to **per-title encoding**: a cartoon with flat colours can look excellent at 1080p for well under the fixed ladder's bitrate, while grainy action footage needs far more. They later moved to **shot-based** encoding, which chooses settings per scene. The pay-off is the same quality for fewer bits, which saves egress on every future view.

### Spending compute where views are

Assume a skewed popularity distribution for this design; measure the actual catalogue before allocating expensive encode work. A sensible policy:

- On upload, encode a fast H.264 ladder so the video is watchable within minutes.
- When a video crosses a view threshold, re-encode it in VP9/AV1. Potential bitrate savings and encoding cost depend on content, encoder settings and quality metrics; benchmark a representative corpus before choosing a migration threshold. Re-encode only when expected egress savings exceed compute, storage and operational costs for supported playback devices.

## Deep dive 2: adaptive bitrate streaming

Progressive download of a single MP4 can't adapt to the network. **Adaptive bitrate (ABR)** streaming encodes the video at several bitrates, splits each into short segments, and lets the **client** choose a rendition per segment.

### HLS and DASH

- **HLS** (Apple) uses a *master playlist* (`.m3u8`) listing the variants, and a *media playlist* per variant listing segment URLs. Apple's HLS authoring specification recommends a target segment duration of 6 seconds.
- **MPEG-DASH** uses an XML *MPD* manifest with the same idea.
- **CMAF** standardises fragmented-MP4 segments, so one set of files can serve both HLS and DASH. This avoids duplicate segment copies when codec, encryption and player compatibility allow both protocols to share them; it does not universally halve total storage.

```
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1000000
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000
1080p/index.m3u8
```

Because segments are plain HTTP objects with immutable URLs, any HTTP cache or CDN can serve them. This is the main reason HTTP streaming won over specialised streaming protocols such as RTMP.

### How the player chooses

- **Throughput-based**: measure how fast recent segments downloaded and pick the highest bitrate below, say, 80% of that. It reacts quickly but oscillates on noisy links.
- **Buffer-based** (Netflix's BBA research): choose the bitrate from buffer occupancy. With a nearly empty buffer, play safe. With a full buffer, go high. Buffer-aware policies can reduce oscillation; compare stability, startup and stalls on representative traces.
- Player implementations vary: many combine bandwidth estimates with buffer or switching constraints. Startup choices depend on their configuration and history.

Segment length is a trade-off. Short segments (2 s) adapt quickly and cut live latency, but they mean more requests and slightly worse compression, because there are more keyframes. Long segments (10 s) are efficient but adapt slowly.

## Deep dive 3: CDN strategy

At about 50 Tbps peak, the CDN *is* the product.

### Netflix Open Connect

Netflix built its own CDN. **Open Connect Appliances (OCAs)** are storage-heavy servers given free of charge to ISPs and installed *inside* their networks or at internet exchange points.

- The **control plane** (catalogue, auth, playback steering, recommendations) runs in AWS.
- The **data plane** (the video bytes) is served almost entirely from OCAs.
- Because the catalogue is curated and popularity is predictable, Netflix **proactively fills** OCAs overnight, during off-peak hours, with what each region is expected to watch tomorrow. Fills are cheap off-peak, and cache-hit video traffic can stay inside a participating ISP’s network; misses and other deployment arrangements still need upstream connectivity.
- At playback, the steering service returns URLs for the OCAs best placed for that client, ranked by health, load and network proximity.

### YouTube-style long tail

YouTube can't predict which of millions of new uploads will be watched, a long-tail design can use **pull-through caching** in tiers; Google Global Cache documents caching popular Google content inside ISP networks:

```
client -> ISP edge cache (e.g. Google
          Global Cache)
       -> regional cache / shield
       -> origin object store
```

The head of the distribution (viral and popular videos) lives at the edge with workload-dependent hit rates. The long tail is fetched from regional caches or origin on demand. An **origin shield** layer collapses many edge misses for the same segment into a single origin fetch.

### Security on the CDN

Manifests and segment URLs carry **signed tokens** with an expiry, so URLs can't be hot-linked forever. Paid content is encrypted (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady DRM), with keys from a separate licence server. For this protected-media path, cache encrypted segments; manifests, metadata and other CDN content need not be encrypted media ciphertext. Validate authorization separately from the shared object cache key.

## View counts and progress

Writing a row per view at 17 M concurrent viewers is wasteful. Players emit heartbeats every few tens of seconds into a stream such as Kafka. A stream processor deduplicates (one view per session, with a product-specific minimum watch time and additional abuse controls), aggregates per video per minute, and writes counters. Displayed counts can lag by minutes. A lag of minutes may be acceptable for a display counter; billing or audit metrics may need another contract.

The numbers show why. 17 M viewers sending a heartbeat every 30 s is about 570,000 events per second. That is a workload to benchmark for the chosen partitioning and durability settings, but a viral video would turn `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1` into a single hot row taking tens of thousands of writes a second. Pre-aggregating in the stream turns that into one write per video per minute.

Watch progress can use a versioned KV record keyed by `(user_id, video_id)`. Define ordering across sessions/devices; client-clock LWW can let a delayed update overwrite newer progress, while taking the maximum position breaks intentional rewinds. It is debounced on the client so it isn't written every second.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Egress cost** dominates. The levers are better codecs, per-title encoding, and ISP-embedded caches that avoid transit fees.
- **Transcode backlog** during spikes. Prioritise short videos and popular creators, and autoscale on queue depth using spot or pre-emptible instances, since tasks are idempotent and retryable.
- **Cold start for the long tail**. The first viewer of an obscure video pays origin latency. Prefetch the first few segments of each rendition into the regional tier.
- **Storage growth** of roughly 2–3 EB/year. Move old, rarely watched renditions to colder tiers, and consider deleting high-bitrate renditions of dead videos and re-transcoding on demand.

## Evolving at 10x

- **500 Tbps peak**: push caches deeper into ISPs (the Open Connect model), and use multicast-like fills between caches.
- **Live streaming**: use LL-HLS or low-latency DASH with partial segments, an ingest tier that accepts RTMP/SRT, and real-time transcoding (no time to split and fan out a finished file).
- **Global metadata**: replicate read-mostly metadata to every region, with a single write region per shard.
- **ML everywhere**: predictive prefetch and quality-per-bit models (Netflix's VMAF metric) to tune the ladder automatically.

## Key takeaways
- The design is dominated by bytes. Estimate peak egress first (tens of Tbps) and let that justify the CDN.
- Upload directly to object storage with a resumable protocol, then drive a queue-backed, idempotent DAG of chunked transcode tasks.
- ABR (HLS/DASH, ideally CMAF) puts the client in charge of choosing bitrates segment by segment, and makes video cacheable by ordinary HTTP caches.
- Spend expensive encoding (AV1, per-title, per-shot) in proportion to popularity. Use a measured break-even model; it need not pay off for every video or device mix.
- A curated catalogue (Netflix) can be proactively pushed to ISP-embedded caches off-peak. A long-tail catalogue (YouTube) needs tiered pull-through caching with an origin shield.

> **Content gap:** no reproducible encoder benchmark, CDN hit-rate measurement or current egress quote is supplied. Capacity, bitrate and cost calculations use explicit scenario inputs. Historical platform descriptions do not establish current internal implementations.

questions.prompt: In an HLS-based video service, what does the `GET /videos/{id}/play` endpoint on your API servers typically return?

options.text: A signed URL to a manifest (master playlist) on the CDN, plus DRM licence details
options.explanation: Correct. The player fetches the manifest from the CDN, picks a rendition and pulls segments over plain HTTP. The API only authorises playback and hands out signed, expiring URLs.

options.text: The video bytes, streamed from the API server over a long-lived HTTP response
options.explanation: Wrong. Streaming tens of Tbps through API servers would be ruinously expensive and slow. The API tier serves only small control-plane responses, and the bytes come from the CDN.

options.text: A WebSocket connection over which the server pushes segments at the right bitrate
options.explanation: Wrong. In HLS/DASH the client pulls segments and decides the bitrate itself. Server push over WebSockets would defeat ordinary HTTP caching, which is the main reason HTTP streaming won.

options.text: A single MP4 URL at the highest bitrate, which the player downscales locally
options.explanation: Wrong. This is progressive download. It can't adapt to the network, so a viewer on 2 Mbps 4G would stall constantly on a 15 Mbps 4K file.

questions.workedExample:
Separate the **control plane** from the **data plane**:

1. Control plane (your API): is this user allowed to watch? Which CDN node should they use? Here is a signed manifest URL valid for a few hours.
2. Data plane (CDN): the player downloads `master.m3u8`, sees the variants (480p at 1 Mbps, 1080p at 5 Mbps, ...), picks one based on measured throughput and buffer, then fetches 6 s segments one by one.

The API response is a few hundred bytes. The video might be gigabytes. Keeping them apart is what lets the API tier stay small while the CDN scales to Tbps.

questions.prompt: You expect 200 M daily viewers, each watching an average of 1 hour at an average 3 Mbps. Peak concurrency is about 2x the daily average. Roughly what peak egress must your delivery tier sustain?

options.text: About 5 Tbps
options.explanation: Wrong, by 10x. This usually comes from dividing by 24 and then forgetting the peak factor, or from slipping a decimal place in the concurrency (0.83 M instead of 8.3 M).

options.text: About 25 Tbps
options.explanation: Close, but this is the *average* (8.3 M x 3 Mbps). Capacity must be planned for peak, which the question puts at 2x average.

options.text: About 50 Tbps
options.explanation: Correct. Average concurrency is 200 M x 1/24 = 8.3 M. Peak is about 17 M. 17 M x 3 Mbps = 51 Tbps.

options.text: About 600 Tbps
options.explanation: Wrong. This assumes all 200 M viewers watch at the same time (200 M x 3 Mbps). Daily viewers are spread across the day, so concurrency is much lower than DAU.

questions.workedExample: 200M viewer-hours/day divided by 24 gives 8.333M average concurrent viewers. At 2× peak and 3Mbps, required peak payload egress is 50Tbps. Daily payload is 270PB. Geographic distribution and network/egress budgets justify a CDN; these figures do not prove a universal data-center limit or a required number of edge sites.

questions.prompt: A2-hour film takes 6 hours in the current serial encode pipeline. Which design exposes parallel work and individually retryable units to reduce completion time?

options.text: Give the job a much larger machine (e.g. 192 cores) and run ffmpeg with more threads
options.explanation: Wrong. A single encoder's parallelism tops out well below that core count because of frame dependencies and lookahead. You'd still wait a long time, and one crash restarts everything.

options.text: Transcode on the fly at the CDN edge when a viewer first requests each segment
options.explanation: Wrong as the main strategy. Edge transcoding adds latency to every cold request, repeats work on every edge node, and needs heavy CPU at thousands of sites. It's occasionally used for niche formats, but not as the primary pipeline.

options.text: Split the source into keyframe-aligned chunks, fan out one idempotent task per chunk and rendition to a worker pool, then stitch the outputs
options.explanation: Split at independently decodable boundaries, align rendition segments and fan out tasks. Speedup depends on encoder scaling, compute capacity and scheduling/assembly overhead;10,800 tasks alone does not imply minutes.

options.text: Only produce a 240p rendition at first, because it encodes fastest
options.explanation: Partially useful (quick low renditions improve time to first watch), but on its own it gives viewers poor quality and doesn't solve the 6-hour wait for the full ladder.

questions.workedExample: 7,200 seconds divided into 4-second units gives 1,800 chunks; six renditions give 10,800 tasks. Dividing 6 serial wall-hours by task count is only an ideal equal-cost model, not a measured per-task runtime. Benchmark compute and I/O, align independently decodable boundaries, version task identities and publish complete outputs atomically before marking ready.

questions.prompt: For an on-demand catalogue served through Netflix Open Connect, which workload properties make proactive off-peak cache filling useful? Select all that apply.

options.text: A curated catalogue allows a selected regional working set to be pre-positioned
options.explanation: A selected regional working set can be placed in advance. The fraction that fits depends on appliance capacity, rendition sizes and regional demand; long-tail services can also prefetch selected content.

options.text: Viewing popularity is predictable a day ahead from regional history and release schedules
options.explanation: Correct. If you can forecast tomorrow's demand, you can push it during off-peak hours, when the links are idle and cheap, rather than pulling at peak.

options.text: Traffic is strongly diurnal, leaving spare network capacity overnight
options.explanation: Correct. Evening peaks and overnight troughs mean fill traffic can use capacity that would otherwise sit idle, keeping peak links free for playback.

options.text: Most content is live, so it must be pushed before anyone requests it
options.explanation: Wrong. The question concerns on-demand assets already available for placement. Future live media does not yet exist to be preloaded.

options.text: Viewers rarely seek, so only the first few minutes of each title need caching
options.explanation: Wrong. The fill places entire titles (all needed renditions). Viewers watch whole episodes and do seek, so first-minutes-only caching would cause misses mid-play.

questions.workedExample: A curated catalogue, regional demand forecasts and off-peak network capacity make proactive placement useful. Open Connect describes ISP appliances and scheduled fill. Do not infer a fixed catalogue size, appliance capacity or universal hit rate from this pattern. A long-tail service can mix demand-driven caching and prefetch; these are not mutually exclusive platform categories.

questions.prompt: Your player uses a purely throughput-based ABR algorithm. Viewers on mobile complain that quality keeps jumping between 480p and 1080p every few seconds. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Switch to a buffer-based or hybrid algorithm that chooses the bitrate mainly from buffer occupancy, with hysteresis
options.explanation: Buffer-aware switching and hysteresis can damp oscillation. Tune them against representative traces; they do not universally eliminate all quality changes or stalls.

options.text: Make segments 1 second long so the player reacts faster
options.explanation: Wrong as a standalone fix. Faster sampling can make an unsmoothed controller more sensitive to noise; it does not add hysteresis. Shorter segments also increase request rate under the same buffering policy.

options.text: Remove the 720p rendition so there are fewer rungs to switch between
options.explanation: Wrong. Fewer rungs make each switch a *bigger* visible jump (480p straight to 1080p) and waste bandwidth. The ladder isn't the cause of the instability.

options.text: Have the server choose the bitrate instead of the client
options.explanation: Moving the decision alone does not solve oscillation. A server-assisted controller could use client telemetry, but still needs a stable policy; server assistance does not inherently prevent cacheable segments.

questions.workedExample:
Diagnose the cause:

- Mobile throughput is noisy. One segment downloads at 8 Mbps and the next at 2 Mbps.
- A throughput rule like 'pick the highest bitrate below 0.8 x the last measured throughput' flips between 5 Mbps (1080p) and 1 Mbps (480p) every segment.

The fix is to use the **buffer** as a shock absorber:

| Buffer | Choice |
|---|---|
| < 10 s | lowest safe rung |
| 10–30 s | step up gradually |
| > 30 s | top sustainable rung |

With 30 s buffered, a 4 s dip doesn't threaten a stall, so there's no reason to drop quality. Add hysteresis (require sustained evidence before switching) to reduce unnecessary switching, then validate the policy on representative network traces.

questions.prompt: Assume hypothetical 40% bitrate savings for AV1 at equal quality, with an extra $0.40 encode cost for a 10-minute video. For a hypothetical $0.01/GB egress rate and 2.5Mbps H.264 stream, how many minutes watched recover that extra cost?

options.text: About 50 minutes watched
options.explanation: Wrong. This misses the conversion from bits to bytes. 2.5 Mbps is 0.31 MB/s, not 2.5 MB/s, so the saving per minute is about 8x smaller than this answer implies.

options.text: About 360 minutes watched (roughly 36 full views)
options.explanation: Wrong. 360 minutes saves only 360 x 7.5 MB = 2.7 GB, which is $0.027 of egress, about 15x short of the $0.40 encode cost. Always finish by multiplying the per-minute saving back out and comparing it with the cost.

options.text: About 5,300 minutes watched (roughly 530 full views)
options.explanation: Correct. One minute at 2.5 Mbps is 18.75 MB. AV1 saves 40%, which is 7.5 MB = 0.0075 GB, or $0.000075 per minute watched. $0.40 / $0.000075 = ~5,333 minutes.

options.text: It never pays off, because CPU is always more expensive than bandwidth
options.explanation: Wrong. The encode is paid **once** but the saving recurs on **every** view. For any popular video the egress saving dominates, which is exactly why platforms re-encode hot videos in AV1.

questions.workedExample: 2.5Mbps x60/8=18.75MB per minute. A40% reduction saves 7.5MB=0.0075GB, worth$0.000075 at the assumed egress price. $0.40/$0.000075=5,333.33 watch-minutes, or about 534 complete 10-minute views. This covers only the stated encode/egress terms and viewers actually receiving AV1; storage, device support and other costs can shift the threshold.

questions.prompt: You must support both Apple devices (HLS) and Android/web players (DASH). Storage and CDN cache footprint are major costs. What packaging approach minimises them?

options.text: Store separate MPEG-TS segments for HLS and separate fMP4 segments for DASH
options.explanation: Wrong. Where compatible players and encryption can share fragmented MP4, separate media copies create avoidable storage and cache duplication; the effect on total storage and hit rate is workload-dependent.

options.text: Repackage on the fly at the edge from a single mezzanine file
options.explanation: Just-in-time packaging is a legitimate technique (used by some origins), but doing it at every edge costs CPU at thousands of sites and still caches two formats. CMAF achieves the saving without per-request work.

options.text: Use only DASH and ship a JavaScript DASH player on iOS Safari
options.explanation: Wrong in practice. Native iOS apps and AirPlay rely on HLS, and FairPlay DRM is built around HLS. Dropping HLS breaks a large share of devices.

options.text: Package once as CMAF (fragmented MP4) segments, and publish both an HLS playlist and a DASH MPD that reference the same files
options.explanation: Compatible CMAF segments can be shared by HLS and DASH manifests when codec, encryption and player support align. This avoids duplicate media copies for that ladder, not universally half of all platform storage.

questions.workedExample: For compatible players, codecs and encryption, both playlists can reference the same immutable .m4s objects. HLS has supported fragmented MP4 as well as MPEG-TS; separate duplicate media is not inherent to the protocol. Sharing files reduces duplicate packaging/cache footprint, but originals, alternate codecs and incompatible DRM combinations remain separate costs.

questions.prompt: A sequential GCS-style resumable upload sends a4GB video in 8MiB chunks, with only one chunk in flight. The connection drops near 3.1GB. What should the client do?

options.text: The app restarts the upload from byte 0, because a partial object in storage may be corrupt
options.explanation: Wrong. Throwing away 3.1 GB on every dropout means a long upload on a flaky link may never finish. Resumable protocols exist precisely to avoid this.

options.text: The app asks the upload endpoint for the last committed offset, then sends only the chunks after it
options.explanation: Query the committed byte range and resume after it. Under the one-chunk-in-flight assumption, at most that 8MiB chunk may need retransmission. S3 multipart uses numbered part records instead of one committed offset.

options.text: The API server buffers the whole upload in memory, so the app can just carry on sending where it thinks it stopped
options.explanation: Wrong twice. Multi-GB bodies shouldn't pass through API servers at all, and the client can't know which in-flight bytes actually arrived, so it must ask the server for the committed offset.

options.text: The app re-sends the last 3.1 GB in parallel streams to make up time
options.explanation: Wrong. Those bytes are already stored. Parallelism helps with the *remaining* parts (S3 multipart allows it), not with re-sending committed data.

questions.workedExample: The server’s committed range, not the client’s sent-byte counter, determines where to resume. For 369 complete 8MiB chunks, the next offset is 369×8,388,608=3,095,396,352 bytes. Resume the GCS session with the appropriate Content-Range. Multiple concurrent parts would require separate recovery accounting; S3 tracks part numbers and ETags.

questions.prompt: Your transcoding pipeline runs on spot instances. A worker is reclaimed halfway through encoding chunk 412 of video `v9` at 720p, and the workflow engine retries the task on another machine. Which design choices make that retry safe? Select all that apply.

options.text: Publish a complete validated object or atomically select an immutable attempt output, rather than expose partial data.
options.explanation: Correct. Readers (the packager) never see a partial segment, and an abandoned temporary object is harmless garbage to clean up later.

options.text: Each attempt writes to a fresh random filename, so two attempts never collide
options.explanation: Wrong. Random names mean a retry leaves orphaned outputs and the packager has to work out which one is real. Deterministic names make the retry idempotent instead.

options.text: The video is only marked `ready` after every task in the DAG has completed
options.explanation: Correct. Marking ready early would publish a manifest pointing at a segment that doesn't exist yet. The DAG's final step is the single place that flips the status.

options.text: Workers increment a shared `chunks_done` counter when they finish
options.explanation: Wrong. A counter increment is not idempotent. A task that finishes, crashes before acknowledging and is retried would count twice, and the video could be marked ready with a chunk missing.

options.text: Include source and encode-profile versions in the task key, and use conditional completion/versioned output publication.
options.explanation: Versioned identities and atomic winning-result selection prevent stale attempts from replacing a newer encode. A fixed filename alone provides no such protection.

questions.workedExample: An interrupted multipart upload is not a completed object. Retry the versioned task, validate its full output and conditionally publish the winning result. S3 has no generic filesystem-style atomic rename; immutable object keys plus an atomic metadata pointer are an option. Track completed task identities rather than blind increments, and publish a ready manifest only after all required outputs exist.

questions.prompt: A music video goes viral with 2 M people watching at once. View counts are stored as `videos.view_count` in the sharded MySQL tier, and each player runs `UPDATE ... SET view_count = view_count + 1` when playback starts. The shard holding that video starts timing out. What is the best fix?

options.text: Move the shard to a bigger machine
options.explanation: Wrong. Every increment to the same row takes the same row lock, so they serialise no matter how many cores you add. A bigger box buys little against a single hot row.

options.text: Re-shard `videos` by a hash of `video_id`
options.explanation: Wrong. The video already lives on exactly one shard, and it's one row. No sharding key spreads writes to a single row.

options.text: Send view events to a log such as Kafka, deduplicate and aggregate per video per minute in a stream processor, and write the totals
options.explanation: Correct. Thousands of increments a second become one write per video per minute. The count lags slightly, which nobody minds, and the stream step can also apply fraud rules such as a minimum watch time.

options.text: Cache the count in Redis and drop the database write
options.explanation: Partly helpful for reads, but with no durable write the count is lost when Redis restarts, and there is still no deduplication or fraud filtering. The log-and-aggregate pattern solves both.

questions.workedExample:
Quantify the hot spot. Suppose 2 M viewers start within about 10 minutes:

```
2,000,000 / 600 s = ~3,300 writes/s
```

all to **one row**. Each increment takes the row lock, writes redo and commits. Even at 1 ms each that saturates the row.

With stream aggregation:

```
Kafka: 3,300 events/s (trivial)
processor: sum per video per minute
DB: 1 write/min for this video
```

That is a reduction of about 200,000x for the hot row, and it gives you a place to dedupe one view per session.

questions.prompt: For a live design that keeps the same approximate number of buffered full segments, what tradeoff follows from reducing segment duration from 6 to 2 seconds?

options.text: It cuts latency with no downside, because segment length only affects the manifest
options.explanation: Wrong. Each segment must start with a keyframe, so shorter segments mean more keyframes (worse compression) and three times as many HTTP requests per viewer.

options.text: It lowers latency, but triples segment requests and costs some compression because every segment starts with a keyframe. LL-HLS partial segments are the usual way to go lower still
options.explanation: It can reduce packaging/buffer delay under the stated policy and triples full-segment request frequency. Compression cost depends on whether random-access/keyframe spacing also changes. LL-HLS publishes partial segments for lower latency.

options.text: It increases latency, because the player must fetch three times as many segments before starting
options.explanation: Wrong. The player buffers a similar *number* of segments, so shorter segments mean less buffered time and lower latency.

options.text: It makes no difference to latency, which is set entirely by the CDN's cache TTL
options.explanation: Wrong. Live latency is dominated by encode and packaging delay plus how much the player buffers, and buffer depth is measured in segments.

questions.workedExample: Full-segment requests increase from 60/6=10 to 60/2=30 per minute, excluding manifests/audio/parts. If encode/package delay is one segment, transport 2 seconds and player buffer three segments, the illustrative latency changes from 26 to 10 seconds. These are chosen assumptions, not universal player behavior. LL-HLS parts can be delivered before a complete segment exists; not every part must be independently decodable.

questions.prompt: An obscure video is suddenly shared by a celebrity. Within a minute, 3,000 edge caches worldwide miss on its first segments at the same moment. Which measures protect the origin object store? Select all that apply.

options.text: Generating a unique signed URL per viewer that is also used as the cache key
options.explanation: If per-viewer token parameters enter the cache key, they fragment the cache. Configure authorization to run before cache delivery and normalize only authorization-only parameters; CDN defaults differ.

options.text: Prefetching the first few segments of each rendition into the regional tier when a video is published
options.explanation: Correct. The opening segments are what every new viewer needs first, so having them warm in the shield removes the worst of the cold start.

options.text: Request collapsing at each cache tier, so concurrent misses for the same object wait on a single upstream fetch
options.explanation: Correct. Without collapsing, 50 simultaneous misses at one shield node would still mean 50 origin fetches. With it, one fetch serves all 50.

options.text: An origin shield (regional cache tier) between the edges and the origin
options.explanation: Correct. Edges miss to a handful of shield nodes rather than to origin, so 3,000 misses become a few origin fetches.

options.text: Lowering segment cache TTLs to a few seconds so caches stay fresh
options.explanation: Wrong. Segments are immutable, so they can be cached for a long time. Short TTLs would *increase* origin traffic by forcing repeated revalidation.

questions.workedExample: For an illustrative burst of 3,000 edge misses and 20 populated shield routes, coalescing can reduce origin fetches toward one per shield. Prefetched resident objects may avoid those fetches. Failures, evictions and routing can increase them. Validate each viewer’s authorization even on hits; do not remove identity-bearing cache-key differences unless the content is truly shareable.

lessons.title: Ride-sharing (Uber / Lyft)
lessons.summary: Design a ride-hailing backend, covering high-rate driver location ingestion, geospatial indexing with geohash, quadtrees, S2 and H3, rider-driver matching, and surge pricing.
lessons.body:
Ride-sharing looks like a booking app, but the core is a **real-time geospatial system**. Millions of moving points update every few seconds, and the hot query is "who is near this spot, right now?". Every trip also needs a strongly consistent state machine so a driver can't be sent to two riders.

## Requirements

### Functional
- Drivers go online and stream their location.
- Riders see nearby cars, request a ride and get a price quote.
- The system matches a rider to a driver. The driver accepts, and both see each other live.
- The trip progresses (en route → arrived → in trip → completed), then payment is taken.
- Prices surge when demand exceeds supply in an area.

### Non-functional
- **Match latency**: a driver offer within a few seconds of the request.
- **Freshness**: locations no more than about 5–10 s stale.
- **Correctness**: a driver is never assigned two trips. A trip is never lost or double-charged.
- **Availability**: the request path must keep working through a data-centre failure. A city with no dispatch is a city with no revenue.
- Location data is high volume but **ephemeral**. Only the latest position matters for matching.

## Back-of-the-envelope

Uber reported nearly 11.3 billion trips for 2024, about 31 M a day, but that figure includes Uber Eats deliveries, so rides alone are a good deal fewer. Design for a large ride-hailing platform:

```
Trips:      20 M/day
  avg  20e6 / 86,400  = ~230/s
  peak (5x, Friday evening) = ~1,200/s
Online drivers at peak: 2 M
Location update every 4 s:
  2e6 / 4 = 500,000 writes/s
Payload ~100 B (id, lat, lng,
  heading, speed, ts, status)
  500k x 100 B = 50 MB/s ingest
```

What matters:

- **500 k writes/s** of location, each overwriting the previous one. A rebuildable in-memory index is a useful design option; durable stores can also handle high write rates when partitioned and provisioned appropriately.
- The latest-location state is tiny: 2 M drivers × ~100 B = **200 MB**. That is raw payload only: geospatial indexes, identifiers, object overhead and replication increase memory. Sharding choices need measured memory and throughput.
- Trip writes are modest (around a thousand a second), but they must be transactional.
- Location history for trip receipts and analytics: 500 k/s × 100 B × 86,400 = about **4.3 TB/day**, streamed to cheap storage.

## API design

```
// driver app (persistent connection)
WS  /v1/driver/stream
  -> {lat, lng, heading, ts}   every 4 s
  <- {type:"offer", trip_id, pickup, ttl}

POST /v1/driver/offers/{trip_id}/accept

// rider app
GET  /v1/quotes?pickup=..&dropoff=..
  -> {quote_id, price, surge, expires_at}
POST /v1/trips
  {quote_id, pickup, dropoff}
  Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
  -> {trip_id, status:"matching"}
GET  /v1/trips/{id}   (or subscribe via WS)
```

The **quote** locks the price, including surge, for a few minutes. That way the rider pays what they were shown, even if surge changes a second later. The **idempotency key** on `POST /trips` stops a flaky network retry from booking two cars.

## Data model

```
// in-memory, sharded by geo cell
driver_loc: driver_id -> {lat,lng,ts,
                          status,cell}
cell_index: cell_id -> set(driver_id)

// durable (sharded SQL / document DB)
trips(trip_id PK, rider_id, driver_id,
      status, quote_id, pickup, dropoff,
      fare, version, created_at)
drivers(driver_id PK, vehicle, rating,
        state, state_version)
```

Trips are sharded by `trip_id` (or by city, for locality). The trip row carries a `version` used for optimistic concurrency on state transitions.

## High-level architecture

```
 Driver app          Rider app
     |                   |
     v                   v
+-----------------------------+
|  Edge / WebSocket gateway   |
+-----------------------------+
   |            |          |
   v            v          v
+--------+ +----------+ +-------+
|Location| | Dispatch | | Trip  |
|service | | /matching| |service|
+--------+ +----------+ +-------+
   |   \        |          |
   v    \       v          v
+------+ \  +-------+  +-------+
| Geo  |  ->| Kafka |  |Trip DB|
|index |    +-------+  +-------+
|(RAM) |        |
+------+        v
          +-----------+
          |Surge, ETA,|
          | analytics |
          +-----------+
```

## Deep dive 1: ingesting locations

Drivers keep a persistent connection (WebSocket, gRPC stream, or MQTT) to a gateway. Persistent streams reduce per-message headers. HTTP keep-alive or HTTP/2 can also reuse TLS connections, so each HTTP update need not incur a handshake.

For each update, the location service:

1. Validates it (drops GPS jumps of 5 km in 4 s, and out-of-order timestamps).
2. Computes the driver's **cell id** at the indexing resolution.
3. Updates `driver_loc`. If the cell changed, it moves the driver between `cell_index` sets.
4. Publishes the update to Kafka for surge, ETA models, fraud checks and trip trails.

The in-memory index is **sharded by cell**, with neighbouring cells grouped onto the same shard where possible. Uber's dispatch system famously sharded geo-state across a consistent-hash ring (their open-source Ringpop library, using SWIM gossip for membership). Historical Ringpop is an example, not a claim about the current entire Uber stack. For this soft-state index, fresh connected-driver pings can rebuild locations after routing recovers. Four seconds is the nominal update interval, not a failover bound; disconnected drivers remain missing. This is a deliberate choice: **soft state** you can afford to lose.

## Deep dive 2: geospatial indexing

The query is "the K nearest available drivers within R km of the rider". A lexicographic B-tree on `(lat,lng)` is not a general efficient radius index. Spatial trees, database spatial indexes or cell mappings can support 2D searches.

### Geohash

Geohash interleaves latitude and longitude bits and base-32 encodes them. Shared prefixes mean nearby cells.

| Length | Approx. width × height near equator |
|---|---|
| 5 | 4.9 km × 4.9 km |
| 6 | 1.2 km × 0.6 km |
| 7 | 153 m × 153 m |

- **Pros**: simple, works as a string key in any KV store or DB. Redis `GEOSEARCH` uses a 52-bit geohash in a sorted set.
- **Cons**: the **edge problem**. Two points a metre apart across a cell boundary can share no prefix, so a radius search must cover every cell intersecting the search area and then filter by exact distance. The centre cell plus eight neighbours is sufficient only when the chosen cell size and search radius justify that coverage. Cells are also rectangles that distort with latitude.

### Quadtree

Recursively split a region into four until each leaf holds at most N points (say 100).

- **Pros**: adapts to density. Central London gets tiny cells and the countryside gets huge ones, which can help manage local density. Query work still depends on radius and the number of results.
- **Cons**: it's an in-memory structure that must be rebalanced as points move. With 500 k moves a second, splitting and merging nodes gets expensive, so it suits slow-changing data (restaurants, shops) better than moving cars.

### S2 (Google)

S2 projects the sphere onto a cube and orders cells along a **Hilbert curve**, which preserves locality better than geohash's Z-order. Cells have 64-bit ids across 31 levels. A circle can be **covered** by a small set of cells at mixed levels, giving a handful of id ranges to scan. Uber's early dispatch sharded by S2 cell.

### H3 (Uber)

H3 tiles the world in **hexagons** across 16 resolutions (0 to 15). Each step down is roughly 7 times smaller in area. Average cell sizes from the H3 docs:

| Resolution | Avg area | Avg edge |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | ~5.2 km² | ~1.4 km |
| 8 | ~0.74 km² | ~530 m |
| 9 | ~0.11 km² | ~200 m |

These are averages: because H3 projects from an icosahedron, hexagon area at one resolution varies by up to about 2x across the globe (excluding the smaller pentagons), though neighbouring cells in one city are very close in size. A sphere can't be tiled with hexagons alone, so each resolution also has 12 pentagons.

- A regular planar hexagon has six equally spaced neighbours. H3 approximates this geometry on a sphere; actual centre distances vary with projection distortion and pentagon boundaries. A square has edge neighbours and corner neighbours at different distances. This makes "k-ring" searches (all cells within k steps) and smoothing across neighbours clean.
- Uber built H3 specifically for surge pricing and supply/demand analysis.

> [!tip] What to say in the interview
> "I'd index drivers by H3 cell at about resolution 8 in an in-memory sharded store. For a request, I take a k-ring around the rider's cell, gather the available drivers, then rank them by road-network ETA, not straight-line distance." That names a real scheme, handles the edge problem, and shows you know crow-flies distance is misleading (think of a river with no bridge).

## Deep dive 3: matching

### Candidate generation and ranking
1. Use a cell neighborhood large enough for the intended search area; a fixed graph radius is only an approximation to a metric radius. Expand candidates as needed and filter/rank by actual distance or ETA.
2. Filter to `status = available` and to the right vehicle type.
3. Ask the **ETA service** (routing on a road graph with live traffic) for the top ~10 by straight-line distance.
4. Rank by ETA, plus factors such as acceptance rate and keeping drivers' earnings fair.

### Offering without double-booking
The crucial correctness property is that **a driver holds at most one offer or trip**. Make driver state an explicit state machine with a compare-and-set:

```
UPDATE drivers
SET state='offered', state_version=v+1
WHERE driver_id=? AND state='available'
  AND state_version=v
```

Only one dispatcher can win that CAS. The offer goes out with a TTL (say 15 s). Bind the offer to a unique offer ID and epoch. A timeout may release only that same still-pending offer; it must not undo a later acceptance or offer. Acceptance must atomically validate and update the driver reservation and trip, or use a recoverable protocol preserving both invariants. Two unrelated CAS operations alone are insufficient.

### Greedy versus batched matching
Greedy matching (each request immediately takes the nearest driver) is locally optimal but globally poor. Two riders a block apart can each grab the driver better suited to the other. An illustrative **batched matching** design collects requests for a short window (say 1–2 s), build a cost matrix of ETAs, and solve the assignment problem (for example, Hungarian-style algorithms). The cost is a little extra latency in exchange for lower average pickup times across the city.

## Deep dive 4: surge pricing

Surge balances the market. Higher prices can influence supply and demand; the size and timing of the response are empirical and market-dependent.

1. A stream job (Flink or Kafka Streams) consumes ride requests (demand) and available-driver pings (supply).
2. Every ~1 minute, per H3 cell (around resolution 7–8), compute demand/supply over a sliding window.
3. **Smooth** across neighbouring hexagons and across time. This reduces abrupt boundary changes; it does not eliminate flicker or strategic behavior.
4. Map the ratio to a multiplier via a pricing model, capped by policy and regulation.
5. Write `cell -> multiplier` to a low-latency KV store that the quote service reads.

The quote service returns a `quote_id` holding the price. `POST /trips` honours it until expiry, which keeps pricing consistent even though surge is eventually consistent.

## Trip lifecycle and reliability

```
requested -> matching -> driver_assigned
  -> driver_arrived -> in_trip
  -> completed -> paid
(cancel possible from early states)
```

Persist every transition durably, using optimistic concurrency. Emit events (outbox pattern) so payments, receipts and notifications react asynchronously. Payment runs *after* the trip on a separate, idempotent path, which can decouple post-trip charging from dispatch. Preauthorisation, risk checks or payment eligibility may still be dependencies in another product policy.

For the live map, the rider subscribes to the driver's location, and the gateway pushes updates every few seconds over the rider's WebSocket. The client interpolates movement between points so the car glides rather than jumps.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Hot cells**: a stadium emptying creates 50 k requests in one hexagon. Finer cells for dense areas, and batching, keep any one shard from melting.
- **Consistency vs availability**: locations are AP (stale by seconds is fine). Driver assignment and trip state are CP (they must never double-book). Mixing the two tiers deliberately is the key insight.
- **Straight-line vs ETA**: ETA calls are expensive, so pre-filter cheaply by cell and call routing only for the top candidates.
- **Mobile networks**: drivers drop out in tunnels. Treat a driver as stale after ~30 s without a ping and exclude them from matching.

## Evolving at 10x

- **5 M writes/s of location**: shard per city or region. Cities are natural failure and scaling domains, since a trip rarely spans two of them.
- **Multi-region**: active cities can be distributed among home regions with standby replicas. For each city, safe failover needs fenced ownership and a defined replication-loss policy. A driver phone may supply recovery evidence but cannot independently prove authoritative trip/payment state.
- **Richer products** (pooling, scheduled rides, deliveries) turn matching into a vehicle-routing problem. Batch windows and optimisation solvers grow in importance.
- **Edge compute**: run dispatch close to users for latency, and keep only aggregates global.

## Key takeaways
- Location ingestion is huge in writes (hundreds of thousands a second) but small in state (hundreds of MB). A sharded in-memory soft-state index is one option; evaluate durable alternatives against measured requirements.
- Map 2D space to keys. Geohash is simple but has the edge problem. Quadtrees adapt to density but suit slowly changing data. S2 and H3 are widely used alternatives with different geometry and hierarchy tradeoffs; H3 neighbor distances are not perfectly uniform on the sphere.
- Rank candidates by road-network ETA, not distance, and consider batched assignment over greedy matching.
- Use conditional state transitions with offer fencing and atomic driver/trip acceptance to prevent double-dispatch. Keep locations eventually consistent.
- Lock surge into a quote with an expiry, so prices stay consistent for the rider even though surge itself is computed asynchronously.

> **Content gap:** no end-to-end dispatch benchmark, exact failover bound or measured matching/surge improvement is supplied. Batch windows, location intervals and price-hold rules here are design assumptions, not verified current Uber/Lyft internals.

## Further reading
- [H3: hexagonal hierarchical geospatial indexing (docs)](https://h3geo.org/docs/)
- [S2 Geometry library](https://s2geometry.io/)
- [Geohash (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geohash)
- [Quadtree (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadtree)
- [Optimistic concurrency control (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimistic_concurrency_control)
- [The System Design Primer](https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

questions.prompt: 2 M drivers are online at peak, and each sends a location every 4 seconds. Roughly what write rate must the location tier handle?

options.text: About 8 M writes/s
options.explanation: Wrong. This multiplies by 4 instead of dividing. Each driver sends one update every 4 s, which is 0.25 updates per second, not 4.

options.text: About 500,000 writes/s
options.explanation: Correct. 2,000,000 drivers / 4 s = 500,000 updates per second.

options.text: About 23,000 writes/s
options.explanation: 23,000/s does not follow from the stated data. Two million updates per day would be about 23/s; two billion per day would be about 23,000/s. The actual interval is 4 seconds.

options.text: About 1,200 writes/s
options.explanation: Wrong. That's roughly the peak *trip request* rate. Location pings outnumber trip requests by more than 400x.

questions.workedExample:
1. Rate per driver = 1 update / 4 s = **0.25 /s**.
2. Total = 2,000,000 x 0.25 = **500,000 writes/s**.
3. Bandwidth: 500 k x ~100 B = **50 MB/s**.
4. State size: only the latest position per driver, 2 M x 100 B = **200 MB**.

So the workload is huge in writes but tiny in state. That points to a sharded **in-memory** index where each write overwrites the last, not a durable OLTP database writing to disk 500 k times a second.

questions.prompt: You index drivers by geohash at precision 6 and answer 'nearby drivers' by looking only at the rider's own cell. Riders standing near cell boundaries report 'no cars available' while the map shows a car 50 m away. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: Query all cells intersecting the required search area, including neighbors across boundaries, then filter by actual distance.
options.explanation: A3×3 neighborhood suffices only when its geometry covers the desired radius at that latitude. Expand beyond immediate neighbors when necessary.

options.text: Geohash precision 6 is too coarse. Switch to precision 9
options.explanation: Wrong. Finer cells make the boundary problem *more* frequent, because more riders sit near an edge. Precision isn't the root cause.

options.text: Geohash cells overlap, so drivers are being double-counted and then removed
options.explanation: Wrong. Geohash cells tile the plane with no overlap. The issue is the opposite: there's a hard boundary that a single-cell lookup can't see past.

options.text: The geohash needs to be stored as an integer rather than a string
options.explanation: Wrong. The representation (base-32 string or interleaved integer bits) doesn't change which points fall in which cell, so it doesn't fix boundary misses.

questions.workedExample: A driver50m across a boundary is invisible to a single-cell lookup. Cover every cell intersecting the desired metric search region, fetch candidates, then distance-filter. Geohash widths shrink with latitude, so the equatorial1.2×0.6km dimensions do not prove coverage everywhere. H3 gridDisk supplies graph-distance neighbors; pentagons and projection distortion mean it is not an exact equal-distance circle.

questions.prompt: Two dispatcher instances, handling two different riders, both select driver D as the best candidate at the same moment. What mechanism most simply guarantees D receives only one offer?

options.text: Rely on the location index: once D is offered, it removes D from the cell set
options.explanation: Wrong. The location index is eventually consistent soft state. Both dispatchers read it before either update lands, so both still see D as available. It can't provide mutual exclusion.

options.text: Let both offers go out and have the driver app reject the second
options.explanation: Wrong. It pushes correctness to an unreliable mobile client. If the driver accepts both quickly, or the app is offline, you now have two riders expecting one car.

options.text: Route all dispatching globally through a single thread
options.explanation: Wrong. It would be correct, but at ~1,200 requests/s with ETA calls per request it's a throughput and availability bottleneck. A single global thread also can't survive a data-centre failure.

options.text: A conditional write (compare-and-set) on D's state: set `offered` only `WHERE state='available' AND version=v`
options.explanation: Correct. Exactly one of the two conditional updates succeeds. The loser sees 0 rows affected and moves to its next candidate. It's simple, has no lock service, and is correct even with retries.

questions.workedExample: Two authoritative CAS updates against available/version 7 cannot both succeed. Bind the winning offer to a unique offer ID and epoch. Only that still-pending offer can be expired or declined; a stale timeout must not release a later accepted trip. Driver reservation and trip acceptance must commit atomically or follow a recoverable protocol preserving both invariants.

questions.prompt: Uber built H3 using hexagons rather than squares. Which advantages of hexagonal cells matter for surge pricing and supply/demand analysis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Regular planar hexagons have six equally spaced edge neighbors, which provides a useful approximation for local H3 smoothing.
options.explanation: H3 approximates this geometry on a sphere; actual distances vary with projection distortion and near pentagons. It does not make every direction exactly equal.

options.text: k-ring queries (all cells within k steps) approximate a circle well
options.explanation: Correct. A hexagonal k-ring is a reasonable approximation of a radius, which suits 'demand within about 1 km'. Square rings are squares, with corners much further away than their edges.

options.text: Hexagons nest perfectly, so each parent is exactly 7 children with no gaps or overlap
options.explanation: Wrong. Hexagons *can't* be tiled exactly by smaller hexagons. H3's children only approximately cover their parent (with a rotation between resolutions). S2's square cells, by contrast, nest exactly.

options.text: Hexagonal cells eliminate the need for any neighbour lookups
options.explanation: Wrong. You still need neighbours. Hexagons just make neighbour relationships uniform and cheap to compute.

options.text: Cells at a given resolution have roughly uniform area, so per-cell supply/demand ratios are comparable
options.explanation: Correct. Neighbouring H3 cells at one resolution are very close in area, unlike lat/lng rectangles, which shrink towards the poles. (Across the whole globe, area at one resolution varies by up to about 2x, but within a city that hardly matters.)

questions.workedExample: Hexagonal graph neighborhoods are useful for local smoothing and approximately circular candidate regions. H3 has projection distortion and twelve pentagons per resolution, so actual distances/areas vary. The roughly 2× global area ratio refers to hexagons only. Parent-child logical hierarchy is exact, while geometric containment is approximate.

questions.prompt: Your greedy dispatcher assigns each request, the moment it arrives, to the driver with the lowest ETA. Average pickup times are worse than a competitor's in dense downtown areas. Which change best addresses this?

options.text: Collect requests over a 1–2 s window, build an ETA cost matrix between those riders and nearby drivers, and solve the assignment problem to minimise total ETA
options.explanation: Batching can improve the assignment objective on the chosen candidates, but adds waiting and computation. Net real-world pickup benefit must be measured;1–2 seconds is a hypothetical window.

options.text: Rank by straight-line distance instead of ETA, because it's cheaper and lets you consider more drivers
options.explanation: Wrong. Straight-line distance ignores one-way streets, rivers and traffic. It's fine for pre-filtering but makes the final ranking worse, not better.

options.text: Increase the location update interval to 15 s to reduce load
options.explanation: Wrong. Staler locations make ETAs less accurate, which worsens matching. Load isn't the problem described.

options.text: Offer each request to the 5 nearest drivers at the same time and take the first acceptance
options.explanation: Wrong. Broadcasting causes the double-booking and fairness problems that CAS state machines prevent. It annoys drivers and still doesn't optimise globally.

questions.workedExample:
A tiny example shows the greedy failure:

| | Driver X | Driver Y |
|---|---|---|
| Rider A | 2 min | 3 min |
| Rider B | 3 min | 10 min |

Greedy: A arrives first and takes X (2 min), so B gets Y (10 min). Total **12 min**.

Batched: A gets Y (3 min) and B gets X (3 min). Total **6 min**.

With a 2 s window downtown, you might batch dozens of riders and drivers and solve with a Hungarian-style or min-cost-flow solver. In quiet suburbs a batch has one rider, so batching degenerates gracefully to greedy.

questions.prompt: Surge multipliers are recomputed every minute per H3 cell. A rider sees £14.00 (1.4x), taps Request 20 seconds later, and surge has risen to 1.8x. What should happen?

options.text: Honour the price via the `quote_id` returned with it, which is valid until its `expires_at`
options.explanation: Correct. Quotes lock the price for a short window (a few minutes). Surge can then be computed asynchronously and eventually consistently, while each rider's price stays consistent.

options.text: Charge 1.8x, because that's the current market price
options.explanation: The displayed unexpired quote is the contract in this scenario. Silently replacing it with a higher price breaks that contract; legal requirements depend on jurisdiction and product terms.

options.text: Recompute surge synchronously at request time so it's always exact
options.explanation: Wrong. Computing demand/supply over sliding windows and neighbours on every request is expensive, and still wouldn't match the price the rider was shown a moment ago.

options.text: Reject the request and force the rider to refresh
options.explanation: Wrong. It's poor user experience and causes extra request churn exactly when demand is highest. A quote with an expiry is the standard pattern.

questions.workedExample:
The design separates two concerns:

1. **Market signal**: the stream job computes `cell -> multiplier` every ~60 s. It's eventually consistent and may change at any moment.
2. **Customer contract**: `GET /quotes` reads the multiplier, computes a price and stores `{quote_id, price, expires_at = now + 2 min}`.
3. `POST /trips {quote_id}` checks the quote exists, is unexpired and belongs to this rider, then uses *its* price.

If the quote has expired, the app fetches a fresh one and shows the new price before confirming. Store quotes in a fast KV store with a TTL, so expiry cleans up automatically.

questions.prompt: One shard of your in-memory location index crashes and loses all its data. What is the impact, and what is the recovery strategy implied by a good design?

options.text: Catastrophic. You must restore it from the last nightly backup
options.explanation: Wrong. A nightly backup of positions that change every 4 s is worthless. The data is stale within seconds, so backing it up is pointless.

options.text: Trips in progress are lost, because trip state lives in the location index
options.explanation: Wrong in a good design. Trip state belongs in a durable, transactional store, separate from soft location state, precisely so a location-shard loss can't lose trips.

options.text: Rebuild the soft-state index from fresh pings once routing recovers, keeping authoritative trip/driver-assignment state in durable storage.
options.explanation: Nominal 4-second updates help recovery for connected drivers, but detection, routing, reconnection and network delays can extend degradation. Missing/stale drivers should be excluded until refreshed.

options.text: Replay the last 24 hours of Kafka location events into the new shard
options.explanation: Wrong. Replaying hours of history is slow and unnecessary. Only the latest point per driver matters, and fresh pings will arrive in 4 s anyway.

questions.workedExample: A shard crash removes candidate locations, not durable trips. Reassign ownership safely, accept fresh sequenced pings and rebuild the geo index. A lost or disconnected device may not refresh promptly; apply a freshness threshold. Optional recent-state replication or log replay can reduce degradation. No measured one-to-four-second recovery guarantee is available.

questions.prompt: Away from H3 pentagon distortions, approximate resolution 8 cells as regular hexagons with average area 0.74km². For graph radiusk=2, about how many cells and total area are covered?

options.text: 9 cells, about 6.7 km²
options.explanation: Wrong. 9 is the geohash answer (a cell plus its 8 square neighbours). A hexagon has 6 neighbours, and a k-ring grows by 6k cells per ring.

options.text: 13 cells, about 9.6 km²
options.explanation: Wrong. This adds 6 for each ring (1 + 6 + 6) but forgets that each ring is longer than the last. Ring k has 6k cells, so ring 2 has 12.

options.text: 19 cells, about 14 km²
options.explanation: Correct. 1 (the centre) + 6 (ring 1) + 12 (ring 2) = 19 cells. 19 x 0.74 km² is about 14 km², roughly a circle of radius 2 km.

options.text: 25 cells, about 18.5 km²
options.explanation: Wrong. 25 is a 5 x 5 square block. Hexagonal rings grow as 1 + 3k(k + 1), not as (2k + 1)².

questions.workedExample:
Count the cells ring by ring. Ring k contains 6k hexagons:

```
k=0: 1
k=1: 6   (total 7)
k=2: 12  (total 19)
```

The general formula is 1 + 3k(k + 1). For k = 2: 1 + 3 x 2 x 3 = **19**.

Area: 19 x 0.74 km² = **~14 km²**. A circle of that area has radius sqrt(14 / 3.14), about 2.1 km.

That's a sensible pickup search in a city. If it comes back empty, expand to k = 3 (37 cells, ~27 km²).

questions.prompt: In this design, which authoritative mutation paths need coordination to prevent conflicting driver assignments and invalid trip transitions? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whether driver D is `available`, `offered` or `on_trip`
options.explanation: The reservation write needs an authoritative atomic guard. Candidate reads can be stale if that guard rejects obsolete choices; the authority can be replicated through consensus rather than one physical copy.

options.text: The surge multiplier per H3 cell
options.explanation: Wrong. Surge is a smoothed market signal recomputed every minute. What has to be consistent is the price the rider accepted, which lives in the quote.

options.text: Each driver's latest latitude and longitude
options.explanation: Wrong. Location is soft state that refreshes every 4 s. A position a few seconds stale only makes the ranking slightly less accurate, and making it CP would add replication cost to 500,000 writes a second.

options.text: Trip state transitions such as `driver_assigned` to `in_trip` to `completed`
options.explanation: Correct. The trip drives payment. A lost or duplicated transition means a lost trip or a double charge.

options.text: Every read of an immutable, signed, rider-bound quote must use a linearizable database.
options.explanation: Not necessarily. An immutable authenticated quote can carry its price, rider, route and expiry; an eventual store must not substitute a different price on a miss. Revocation or single-use redemption can require coordination, but ordinary quote reads need not all be linearizable.

questions.workedExample: Coordinate driver reservation and authoritative trip-state changes. Candidate locations, surge estimates and display reads can be stale under explicit policies. An immutable signed quote can preserve the offered price without a linearizable lookup; validate identity, route and expiry, and coordinate redemption if the product requires it.

questions.prompt: At peak you handle about 1,200 ride requests a second, and a k-ring search in a busy city returns around 300 available drivers. A teammate wants to call the road-routing ETA service for all 300 candidates. What's the better approach?

options.text: Call ETA for all 300, because straight-line distance is misleading
options.explanation: Wrong. Distance is misleading for the final ranking, but routing every candidate costs 1,200 x 300 = 360,000 route computations a second, mostly for drivers who were never going to win.

options.text: Skip ETA entirely and rank by straight-line distance
options.explanation: Wrong. A driver 300 m away across a river with no bridge can be 15 minutes away by road. Crow-flies distance alone gives bad matches.

options.text: Pre-filter cheaply by straight-line distance (and vehicle type), then call ETA only for the top ~10 and rank those
options.explanation: Correct. The cheap filter cuts ETA load by about 30x (12,000 calls/s instead of 360,000), and the expensive ETA call is spent only where it changes the decision.

options.text: Precompute ETAs between every pair of H3 cells once a day
options.explanation: Wrong. ETAs depend on live traffic, and the number of cell pairs is enormous. Cached cell-to-cell estimates can help as a coarse filter, but they can't replace live routing for the final choice.

questions.workedExample: Routing all 300 candidates at 1,200 requests/s means 360,000 route computations/s. A top 10 shortlist reduces that to 12,000, a30× reduction. This trades candidate recall for cost: the best ETA may lie outside the distance shortlist, especially around rivers or limited crossings. Measure recall and widen or improve the coarse filter where needed.

questions.prompt: A rider taps Request. The `POST /v1/trips` reaches the server and a trip is created, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app retries automatically. What stops the rider ending up with two cars?

options.text: The client sends the same `Idempotency-Key` on the retry, and the server returns the existing trip for that key instead of creating another
options.explanation: Correct. The server stores key to trip_id when it first creates the trip. The retry finds the key and gets the original response back.

options.text: The server rejects any second request from the same rider within 60 seconds
options.explanation: Wrong. This blocks legitimate cases (a rider booking for a friend, or cancelling and rebooking) and still returns an error rather than the trip the rider actually has.

options.text: The driver CAS prevents it, because a driver can only hold one trip
options.explanation: Wrong. The CAS stops one *driver* getting two trips. Two duplicate trips would simply be matched to two different drivers.

options.text: TCP guarantees the request is only delivered once
options.explanation: Wrong. TCP guarantees ordering within one connection. After a network switch the retry travels on a new connection, and the server can't tell it from a new request without an application-level key.

questions.workedExample:
Walk the timeline:

```
t0 POST /trips  key=K1
t1 server: insert trip T1, save K1->T1
t2 response lost (network switch)
t3 retry POST /trips  key=K1
t4 server: K1 exists -> return T1
```

The key is generated **once per user intent** (one tap of Request), not per HTTP attempt. Save the key and the trip in the same transaction, so a crash between them can't leave a trip with no key.

questions.prompt: A stadium empties after a concert, and about 50,000 ride requests arrive from a handful of H3 cells within 15 minutes. The shard owning those cells is overloaded. Which measures help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use batched matching for the area, assigning many riders to many drivers per window
options.explanation: Correct. Batching amortises work over each window and produces much better assignments when demand is dense.

options.text: Route every request in the city to one global dispatcher so nothing is double-booked
options.explanation: Wrong. Double-booking is already prevented by the driver CAS. Centralising dispatch would turn a hot shard into a hot *system*.

options.text: Let surge rise in those cells, which draws in drivers and spreads out demand
options.explanation: Higher prices may affect supply and demand, but the response is not immediate or guaranteed. Admission controls and technical capacity protection are still required.

options.text: Index dense areas at a finer resolution so the hotspot spans more cells, which can live on different shards
options.explanation: Finer cells can distribute a spatially broad hotspot if shard placement separates them. A co-located crowd can remain hot, and queries across more cells add fan-out; refinement is not an automatic load split.

options.text: Ask drivers' apps to send locations every second instead of every 4 s
options.explanation: Wrong. That quadruples location writes into the same overloaded cells and doesn't add a single driver.

questions.workedExample:
Size the spike:

```
requests: 50,000 / 900 s = ~55/s
waiting riders: tens of thousands,
  each app polling 'nearby cars'
  every few seconds = ~10,000 reads/s
```

The request rate alone looks modest, but it all lands on one shard, and each request triggers k-ring scans, CAS attempts and ETA calls over the same few cells. On top of that, every waiting rider's map is reading the same cells, and arriving drivers are writing to them.

The fixes attack different parts of the problem:

- **Finer cells** spread the *index* load across shards.
- **Batching** spreads the *matching* work over fewer, better decisions.
- **Surge** changes the *market*, adding supply and smoothing demand.

More frequent pings and a central dispatcher both make the hotspot worse.

lessons.title: Web crawler
lessons.summary: Design a distributed crawler for billions of pages, covering the URL frontier, politeness and robots.txt, dedup with Bloom filters and SimHash, spider traps, and partitioning by host.
lessons.body:
A web crawler sounds simple: fetch a page, extract the links, repeat. At a billion pages, the interesting problems are all about **restraint and memory**. Don't hammer anyone's server. Don't fetch the same thing twice. Don't fall into infinite URL spaces. Decide what to fetch *next* out of tens of billions of candidates.

## Requirements

### Functional
- Start from seed URLs and discover pages by following links.
- Fetch HTML (optionally render JavaScript for some sites), and store the content and metadata for downstream indexing.
- Re-crawl pages to keep them fresh.

### Non-functional
- **Politeness**: obey robots.txt, and never overload a host (at most about one request at a time per host, spaced out).
- **Scale**: 1 B pages per month at first, growing 10x.
- **Robustness**: survive malformed HTML, slow servers, spider traps and crashes, without losing frontier state.
- **Prioritisation**: important and fresh pages first. The web is effectively infinite, so you never finish.
- **Extensibility**: new content types and processors can be plugged in.

## Back-of-the-envelope

```
1 B pages / month
  / (30 x 86,400 s) = ~400 pages/s
  peak/headroom: plan 1,000 pages/s

Avg HTML page ~100 KB (uncompressed)
  400 x 100 KB = 40 MB/s = ~320 Mbps
Storage: 1e9 x 100 KB = 100 TB/month
  (~25 TB compressed)
```

Bandwidth is modest. The hard numbers are about **URLs**. Each page has dozens of outlinks, so the set of *discovered* URLs grows far faster than the set of fetched pages. Plan for about 10 B known URLs.

```
Seen-URL set, exact:
  10e9 x ~100 B = ~1 TB (disk/KV)
Seen-URL Bloom filter, 1% false positives:
  ~9.6 bits/URL x 10e9 = ~12 GB, k=7
```

A 12 GB Bloom filter fits in RAM, split across a few nodes. An exact 1TB set usually motivates disk-backed or distributed storage; it is not inherently impossible to keep it in a large RAM cluster. This trade-off returns in the dedup section.

**Latency drives concurrency.** A fetch takes about 1 s on average (DNS + TCP + TLS + download), so 1,000 pages/s means about **1,000 requests in flight**. Use async I/O (epoll, an event loop) rather than a thread per request.

## API and interfaces

A crawler has few public APIs. What matters is the **internal contracts**.

```
POST /v1/seeds        {urls:[...], priority}
GET  /v1/status/{host}
  -> {queued, fetched, errors, last_fetch}

// fetcher -> storage, per page
{url, final_url, status, fetched_at,
 headers, content_hash, simhash,
 body_ref (WARC offset), outlinks:[...]}
```

Store raw responses in **WARC** files, the standard web-archive format used by Common Crawl and the Internet Archive. These are large append-only files in object storage, with an index of `url -> (file, offset)`.

## Data model

```
url_state(url_hash PK, url, host,
          last_fetch, next_fetch,
          etag, last_modified,
          content_hash, change_rate,
          priority)
host_state(host PK, robots_rules,
           robots_fetched_at, crawl_delay,
           next_allowed_at, ip, error_rate)
```

Both are partitioned by **host**, for reasons explained below.

## High-level architecture

```
          +--------+
 seeds -->|  URL   |<-----------------+
          |frontier|                  |
          +--------+                  |
              |                       |
              v                       |
          +--------+   +-------+      |
          |Fetcher |<->|DNS    |      |
```
